instrument.full_name: Exchange of Notes (June 9 and 10, 1939) between Canada and the United States of America relating to the Application and Interpretation of an Agreement which was embodied in an Exchange of Notes by His Majesty's Minister at Washington and the United States Secretary of State concerning the Naval Forces to be maintained on the Great Lakes
instrument.depositary: None (bilateral exchange of notes). Filed and recorded with the UN Secretariat at the request of the United States on 6 November 1952 (UNTS vol. 149, No. 476).
instrument.key_non_parties: The exchange binds only Canada and the United States. The United Kingdom, which concluded the 1817 Rush-Bagot Agreement with the United States, did not take part in this exchange.
instrument.duration_clause: Neither note states a term. The exchange interprets the 1817 agreement, which either party may terminate on six months' notice; the 1939 notes do not say whether the interpretations would survive such a termination. The 4-inch guns may be mounted only in the summer training season (Skelton note of 10 June 1939, para. 8).
instrument.withdrawal_clause: The notes contain no withdrawal clause. The six-month termination clause of the 1817 agreement applies to that agreement, not expressly to this exchange.
instrument.amendment_clause: No amendment clause. Canada stated that new practical measures concerning naval vessels on the Great Lakes should be settled, as in the past, by consultation and correspondence (Skelton note of 10 June 1939, para. 3). The parties used that route on 30 October and 2 November 1940, agreeing a further interpretation that relaxed the 1939 condition that no armament be installed on Great Lakes-built vessels until they reached the seaboard.
instrument.entry_into_force_requirements: No requirement is stated in the notes. The exchange came into force on 10 June 1939 by the exchange of the notes (UNTS vol. 149, p. 334, note 1; Canada Treaty Information E101663; US Treaties in Force 2025).
instrument.count_basis: No numbered articles: two notes, the Roper note of 9 June 1939 (20 paragraphs) and the Skelton note of 10 June 1939 (10 paragraphs), counted consecutively, excluding salutations, the table of vessels and the block quotation (which is counted within para. 17 of the Roper note). Word count (wc) covers body text, closings and signatures of both notes on the English text published by Canada (Treaty Information E101663), excluding titles, date lines, address blocks, run-in headings and the 34-word vessel table. Headings (1) to (4) follow the numbering in the UNTS text.
instrument.weapons_systems_limited: Naval vessels of Canada and the United States on the Great Lakes: the exchange allows two 4-inch guns on each of three training vessels (all other armament removed, guns dismantled outside the summer training season) and the construction on the Lakes of naval vessels intended only for tidewater service, subject to advance information, removal on completion and no armament until the seaboard.
instrument.key_provisions: Vessels may move freely in the Great Lakes and be maintained at any port there (Roper note, para. 11; Skelton note, para. 6). Reserve training and other normal activity, including target practice, are within the 1817 agreement if conducted in each party's own territorial waters (Roper, para. 12; Skelton, para. 7). Two 4-inch guns may be placed on each of three vessels, all other armament removed, firing confined to the party's territorial waters and the guns dismantled except in the summer training season (Roper, para. 15; Skelton, para. 8). Naval vessels intended only for tidewater service may be built in Great Lakes shipyards, with full information given before construction, removal from the Lakes on completion, and no armament until the seaboard (Roper, para. 19; Skelton, para. 9). Canada consented to the Sacramento replacing the Hawk (Skelton, para. 5). Canada's reply states its assumption that these understandings apply equally to Canadian vessels and shipyards (Skelton, para. 10); the United States did not separately confirm this in the exchange.
instrument.behavior_change: The exchange relaxed rather than tightened the 1817 limits: it accepted armament and shipbuilding on the Lakes that the parties described as not strictly consistent with the agreement's technical scheme, under conditions. Whether and when the United States fitted 4-inch guns, replaced the Hawk with the Sacramento, or built vessels on the Lakes under these terms was not established in the sources reviewed.
instrument.historical_background: On 31 January 1939 the Acting Secretary of the Navy, Admiral Leahy, asked Secretary of State Hull whether two 4-inch guns could be mounted on each US naval vessel on the Great Lakes for reserve training and, if not, whether the Rush-Bagot Agreement could be modified (Roper note of 9 June 1939, para. 1). Hull judged formal modification undesirable because of the agreement's symbolic value (para. 2), and the US Minister in Ottawa, Daniel C. Roper, set out proposed interpretations to the Canadian Under-Secretary of State for External Affairs, O. D. Skelton. Skelton replied on 10 June 1939 that Canada agreed, stating Canada's understanding that the measures would apply equally to Canadian vessels and shipyards.

overview_md: The exchange of notes of 9 and 10 June 1939 between the United States Minister in Ottawa, Daniel C. Roper, and the Canadian Under-Secretary of State for External Affairs, O. D. Skelton, records agreed interpretations of the 1817 Rush-Bagot Agreement on naval forces on the Great Lakes. Rather than amend an agreement whose technical scheme both governments regarded as out of date, they agreed that certain practical measures were consistent with its underlying objective: free movement of naval vessels within the Lakes, reserve training and target practice in each party's own territorial waters, two 4-inch guns on each of three training vessels in the summer season, and the construction in Great Lakes shipyards of naval vessels intended only for tidewater service, subject to advance information, removal on completion and no armament until the seaboard. Canada's reply states its assumption that the understandings apply equally to Canadian vessels and shipyards; the United States did not separately confirm this in the exchange. The exchange entered into force on 10 June 1939 and is listed as in force in the US [Treaties in Force](https://www.state.gov/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/Treaties-in-Force-2025-FINAL.pdf) as of 1 January 2025. It shows the two governments adapting the 1817 agreement by agreed interpretation rather than revision, and further interpretive exchanges followed in 1940, 1942 and 1946.
provisions_md:
The instrument has no numbered articles. Citations refer to paragraphs counted consecutively in the [Roper note of 9 June 1939 and the Skelton note of 10 June 1939](https://treaties.un.org/doc/Publication/UNTS/Volume%20149/v149.pdf#page=358) (UNTS vol. 149, No. 476; also [Canada Treaty Information E101663](https://www.treaty-accord.gc.ca/text-texte.aspx?id=101663&lang=eng)). Headings (1) to (4) are those of the notes. The parties described these measures as consistent with the underlying objective of the 1817 agreement, though in part not strictly consistent with its technical scheme or definitions (Skelton note, para. 3); they are interpretations, not amendments.

### Disposition and functions of vessels
- The naval vessels of each party may move freely in the Great Lakes and be maintained at any of its ports there, notwithstanding the 1817 allocation of vessels by lake (Roper note, para. 11; Skelton note, para. 6).
- Employing the vessels of both parties in reserve training or any other normal activity, including target practice, is within the letter and spirit of the agreement when done within each party's own territorial waters (Roper note, para. 12; Skelton note, para. 7).

### Armament
- Two 4-inch guns may be placed on each of three US naval vessels on the Lakes, with all other armament removed (Roper note, para. 15; Skelton note, para. 8). The 1817 text allows one 18-pound cannon per vessel; Roper noted that a 4-inch gun fires a shell of about 30 pounds (para. 14).
- Conditions: target practice is confined to the party's territorial waters, and the 4-inch guns are dismantled except in the summer season while naval reserves are trained (Roper note, para. 15; Skelton note, para. 8).
- Canada stated its assumption that it would be told the names of the vessels so armed and given particulars of any later change in the armament of the five US vessels (Skelton note, para. 8).

### Construction of naval vessels on the Lakes
- Either country may permit naval vessels intended only for tidewater service to be built in Great Lakes shipyards (Roper note, paras. 16 to 19; Skelton note, para. 9), reading the 1817 bar on building vessels of war on the Lakes in the light of the then absence of a navigable connection to the ocean (Roper note, paras. 17 and 18).
- Conditions: full information to the other government before construction begins; immediate removal from the Lakes on completion; no armament installed until the vessel reaches the seaboard (Roper note, para. 19; Skelton note, para. 9). Removal through the other party's waters requires the usual request through diplomatic channels (Skelton note, para. 9).
- The no-armament condition was relaxed by the [further interpretation of 30 October and 2 November 1940](https://www.treaty-accord.gc.ca/text-texte.aspx?id=101664&lang=eng), a separate instrument.

### Number of vessels
- Canada agreed to the substitution of the Sacramento for the Hawk, assuming it would receive information on both vessels and a formal request for passage (Roper note, para. 9; Skelton note, para. 5).
- The exchange sets no new ceiling on the number or size of vessels. The United States stated that it did not propose to exceed its five vessels, excluding vessels retained immobile as floating barracks, and that it would continue to station only unclassified vessels with a draft of not more than fourteen feet (Roper note, paras. 8 and 10); these are statements of US policy, not reciprocal undertakings. Canada's reply noted only that no increase in the number of US vessels was proposed (Skelton note, para. 5).

### Bound parties
- Although several measures are stated for US vessels, Canada's reply states its assumption that the observations and understandings apply equally to Canadian vessels on the Lakes and to vessels built in Canadian shipyards (Skelton note, para. 10); the United States did not separately confirm this in the exchange. The measures are coded as applying to both parties on that basis, except the Sacramento substitution, which concerns the United States alone, and the information on vessels fitted with 4-inch guns, which Canada assumed the United States would supply (Skelton note, para. 8).
participation_md:
- **Form and parties.** A bilateral exchange of notes at Ottawa between the United States Minister to Canada, Daniel C. Roper (9 June 1939), and the Canadian Under-Secretary of State for External Affairs, O. D. Skelton (10 June 1939) ([Canada Treaty Information, details](https://www.treaty-accord.gc.ca/details.aspx?id=101663&lang=eng)). Roper's note asked for Canada's observations for Secretary Hull's "informal and confidential information" (Roper note, para. 20), and Skelton called it an "informal letter" (Skelton note, para. 1). Both governments nonetheless published it as a treaty: Canada in the Canada Treaty Series (1940 No. 12) and the United States in TIAS 1836 and 61 Stat. 4069, as listed in [Treaties in Force 2025](https://www.state.gov/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/Treaties-in-Force-2025-FINAL.pdf) (Canada, Defense, p. 62). The [Foreign Relations of the United States](https://history.state.gov/historicaldocuments/frus1939v02/ch13subch8) series calls it an understanding effected by exchange of notes.
- **Entry into force.** No requirement is stated. The exchange came into force on 10 June 1939 by the exchange of the notes ([UNTS vol. 149, p. 334, note 1](https://treaties.un.org/doc/Publication/UNTS/Volume%20149/v149.pdf#page=358)).
- **Duration and withdrawal.** The notes state no term and contain no withdrawal clause. They interpret the 1817 agreement, which either party may terminate on six months' notice; the notes do not say how such a termination would affect these interpretations. The 4-inch guns may be mounted only in the summer training season (Skelton note, para. 8).
- **Amendment and later practice.** There is no amendment clause. Canada stated that new practical measures should be settled, as in the past, by consultation and correspondence (Skelton note, para. 3), and the 1940 notes record that this procedure had been agreed ([Skelton note of 30 October 1940, para. 2](https://www.treaty-accord.gc.ca/text-texte.aspx?id=101664&lang=eng)).
- **Review and depositary.** No review mechanism and no depositary. The United States filed and recorded the exchange with the UN Secretariat on 6 November 1952 ([UNTS vol. 149, No. 476](https://treaties.un.org/doc/Publication/UNTS/Volume%20149/v149.pdf#page=356)).
- **Status.** Listed as in force in Treaties in Force as of 1 January 2025.
history_md:
### Origins
On 31 January 1939 the Acting Secretary of the Navy, Admiral Leahy, asked Secretary of State Hull in a confidential letter whether two 4-inch guns could be mounted on each US naval vessel on the Great Lakes for reserve target practice, and if not, whether the Rush-Bagot Agreement could be modified (Roper note of 9 June 1939, para. 1, [UNTS vol. 149, p. 334](https://treaties.un.org/doc/Publication/UNTS/Volume%20149/v149.pdf#page=358); the letter itself was not printed by the Department of State, note 4). Hull concluded that modification was undesirable: the agreement's provisions had long been out of date from a naval standpoint, but it had acquired symbolic importance, and drafts of changes exchanged after the First World War had never been agreed (Roper note, para. 2).

### The US note and the Canadian reply
Roper's note acknowledged that the agreement had "from time to time" been subjected to "what may have been considered technical violations by both parties", and that the five US vessels then on the Lakes, all over 100 tons, "may not be considered entirely in keeping with a literal interpretation", while noting that they were there with Canada's knowledge (Roper note, paras. 3 to 5 and 10). These are qualified US statements, not an acknowledged breach. Roper then proposed interpretations under four headings and on shipbuilding ([UNTS, pp. 338-342](https://treaties.un.org/doc/Publication/UNTS/Volume%20149/v149.pdf#page=362)).

Skelton replied on 10 June 1939 after consulting the Acting Prime Minister and Secretary of State for External Affairs and the Department of National Defence. Canada agreed that formal revision was impracticable, accepted each measure as consistent with the agreement's underlying objective, and stated its assumption that the understandings would apply equally to Canadian vessels and shipyards (Skelton note, paras. 1 to 10, [UNTS, pp. 344-348](https://treaties.un.org/doc/Publication/UNTS/Volume%20149/v149.pdf#page=368); [Canada Treaty Information E101663](https://www.treaty-accord.gc.ca/text-texte.aspx?id=101663&lang=eng)).

### Later operation
On 30 October and 2 November 1940 the governments agreed a further interpretation, expressly referring to the 1939 notes, that allowed armament to be installed on vessels built on the Lakes if it was incapable of immediate use while they remained there ([Canada Treaty Information E101664](https://www.treaty-accord.gc.ca/text-texte.aspx?id=101664&lang=eng)). The Canadian note of 18 November 1946 recalled that notes had been exchanged in 1939, 1940 and 1942 and that both governments recognised the agreement's detailed provisions as inapplicable to present-day conditions ([Canada Treaty Information E101665](https://www.treaty-accord.gc.ca/text-texte.aspx?id=101665&lang=eng); [UNTS vol. 149, p. 3](https://treaties.un.org/doc/Publication/UNTS/Volume%20149/v149.pdf#page=27)). The United States filed and recorded the 1939, 1940 and 1942 exchanges with the UN Secretariat on 6 November 1952 ([UNTS vol. 149, No. 476](https://treaties.un.org/doc/Publication/UNTS/Volume%20149/v149.pdf#page=356)).

Whether the United States fitted 4-inch guns on three vessels, replaced the Hawk with the Sacramento, or notified Canada of the vessels concerned was not established in the sources reviewed. No compliance allegation or formal finding concerning this exchange was identified in the sources reviewed.

coding_notes.note: Taken from Canada's Treaty Information record (E101663), which describes the whole exchange. US Treaties in Force 2025 lists it as 'Agreement relating to the construction of naval vessels on the Great Lakes (interpretation of the Rush-Bagot Agreement)', and UNTS vol. 149 (No. 476) as an exchange of notes relating to the application and interpretation, with respect to the construction of naval vessels on the Great Lakes, of the Agreement of 28 and 29 April 1817; both titles name only one of its subjects.

Coded Legally binding. The notes are styled as informal letters (Roper note, para. 20; Skelton note, para. 1), but Canada published the exchange in its Treaty Series, the United States published it in TIAS and the Statutes at Large, filed it with the UN Secretariat as an agreement, and lists it in Treaties in Force.

Coded interprets AC-108 because both governments presented the measures as consistent with the 1817 agreement's objective rather than as a revision (Roper note, para. 2; Skelton note, paras. 2 and 3), and the Canadian title calls it an exchange relating to the application and interpretation of that agreement.

Set to the date the exchange was completed, following the convention used for the parent exchange of notes (AC-108); a bilateral exchange of notes is not opened for signature in the multilateral sense.

Coded Diplomatic channels only from the instrument's own text: the Skelton note (para. 3) states that new practical measures concerning naval vessels on the Lakes should be settled by consultation and correspondence, and the 1940 Skelton note (para. 2) records that this procedure was agreed.

Coded Yes from the instrument's own text under the codebook definition (data submitted to another party): each government is to provide the other with full information on naval vessels to be built at Great Lakes ports before construction begins (Roper note, para. 19; Skelton note, para. 9).

Notifications: advance information on construction (Skelton note, para. 9) and Canada's stated assumption that it would be informed of the vessels fitted with 4-inch guns and of later armament changes (Skelton note, para. 8).

Not specified in text (instrument's own text). The consultation-by-correspondence procedure in the Skelton note, para. 3, concerns new practical measures, not disputes over interpretation or application.
Not specified in text, coded from the instrument's own text; the same applies to national_authority, technical_cooperation and third_party_roles.
Not specified, from the instrument's own text. The parent agreement's six-month termination clause is not repeated in the notes, so withdrawal_type is None stated for this record.
Risk reduction & CBMs added for the advance-information requirement on shipbuilding, a transparency measure; the main subject remains arms limitation.
Sea, following the coding of the parent record for naval forces on the Great Lakes (inland waters).

Each measure is coded as binding both parties because the Skelton note, para. 10, applies the understandings expressed for US vessels and shipyards equally to Canadian ones. US statements on not increasing its five vessels and on stationing only unclassified vessels of not more than fourteen feet draft (Roper note, paras. 8 and 10) are statements of US policy and are not coded as provisions. The armament row's value of 2 is guns per vessel; the limit of three vessels is stated in its unit.

The 9 June 1939 note is coded Other and the completion of the exchange on 10 June 1939 as Adoption. Roper's reference to possible technical violations is described in prose, not coded as an acknowledged breach, because it is expressly qualified.

research_notes: UNTS vol. 149 retrieved from treaties.un.org (v149.pdf). No. 476 (filed and recorded, 6 November 1952) groups the 1939, 1940 and 1942 exchanges; the 1939 English text runs on even pages 334-348 with Canada's French translation on facing odd pages; title pages are pp. 332-333.
